typical_applications: Budget kitchenware, railway coach panels, trims, general fabrication
trade_off_notes: Cheapest austenitic option here; noticeably weaker corrosion resistance than 304 — keep it indoors/dry.

typical_applications: Utensils, railway coach bodies, general fabrication, decorative trim
trade_off_notes: Jindal's high-volume low-cost grade (variants: 202 JSL AUS, 202 DDQ); good value, but 304-level looks with 200-series corrosion resistance.

typical_applications: Springs, structural trim, railway car structures, conveyor components
trade_off_notes: Work-hardens well for extra spring-back strength; a step up in corrosion resistance from the 200-series.

typical_applications: Kitchen equipment, architecture, food processing, general fabrication, railings
trade_off_notes: The all-purpose baseline grade — balanced cost, corrosion resistance and strength; most other grades get compared against this one.

typical_applications: Welded pressure vessels, pharma/chemical equipment, heavy-weld assemblies
trade_off_notes: Low-carbon 304 — slightly lower strength, but resists weld-zone corrosion where 304 wouldn't.

typical_applications: Marine hardware, chemical processing, coastal architecture, medical instruments
trade_off_notes: Added molybdenum gives real chloride/pitting resistance over 304 — the standard pick for coastal or marine exposure, at a real cost premium.

typical_applications: Pharmaceutical/surgical equipment, offshore fittings, welded marine components
trade_off_notes: Low-carbon 316 — the go-to for heavily welded marine or medical parts where weld-zone corrosion must be avoided.

typical_applications: Exhaust manifolds, aerospace ducting, high-temperature chemical equipment
trade_off_notes: Titanium-stabilized so it resists sensitization above ~425°C — chosen wherever 304-level corrosion resistance is needed at sustained high heat.

typical_applications: Furnace parts, kilns, heat-treatment equipment, boiler baffles
trade_off_notes: Built for sustained high-temperature oxidation resistance, not wet-environment corrosion — not the pick for outdoor/marine use.

typical_applications: Furnace components, radiant tubes, heat exchangers, incinerator liners
trade_off_notes: One of the highest continuous-service temperature ratings here — priced accordingly.

typical_applications: Sulfuric acid handling, flue-gas desulfurization, aggressive-chloride chemical/offshore plants
trade_off_notes: The most corrosion-resistant grade in this sheet, and the priciest — reserve it for environments that genuinely defeat 316L.

typical_applications: Automotive exhaust systems, heat shields, non-critical structural trim
trade_off_notes: The cheapest practical grade here — fine for dry heat exposure, but weaker corrosion resistance than any austenitic grade; avoid wet/salty use.

typical_applications: Kitchen appliance panels, automotive trim, indoor/dry architectural cladding
trade_off_notes: Good bright finish and low cost, but lower ductility and corrosion resistance than any 300-series grade — a common indoor value-engineering swap.

typical_applications: Automotive exhaust, water heaters, architectural trim needing better welds than 409
trade_off_notes: A stabilized 409/430 hybrid — better weld integrity and slightly better corrosion resistance for a modest cost step up.

typical_applications: Cutlery, turbine blades, fasteners, pump shafts
trade_off_notes: Can be heat-treated to high hardness, unlike anything else in this sheet — but has the weakest corrosion resistance; pick it for wear resistance, not corrosion.

typical_applications: Chemical tankers, offshore platforms, pressure vessels needing high strength + corrosion resistance
trade_off_notes: Roughly double the yield strength of 316L at similar corrosion resistance — lets you use thinner, lighter sections, but is harder to form and costs more per kg.

typical_applications: Structural/architectural members, bridges, tanks where full 2205 strength isn't needed
trade_off_notes: A lower-alloy duplex — keeps most of 2205's strength advantage over 316L at a smaller cost premium.
